items.readable_text:
Content:
Remember the following three standard elementary row operations:

Content:
I. Swapping two rows
II. Multiplying a row by a non-zero number
III. Adding a multiple of one row to another row

Content:
Of these three elementary row operations, only III (adding a multiple of one row to another row) preserves the determinant. The other two operations, switching two rows or multiplying a row by a non-zero number, change the determinant.

Content:
To demonstrate, let's consider the matrix [MATH: [1|2; 3|4]] Taking the determinant, we have
[MATH: 1|2; 3|4]

Content:
If we swap the two rows, we get a different determinant:
[MATH: |3|4; 1|2||= 3 ⋅ 2 − 1 ⋅ 4; = 2; ≠ − 2×]

Content:
Likewise, if we multiply top row by [MATH: {\color{red}2},] then we get a different determinant:
[MATH: |2 ⋅ 1|2 ⋅ 2; 3|4||=|2|4; 3|4|; = 2 ⋅ 4 − 3 ⋅ 4; = − 4; ≠ − 2×]

Content:
However, if we add twice the top row to the bottom row, then we get the same determinant:
[MATH: |1|2; 3 + 2 ⋅ 1|4 + 2 ⋅ 2||=|1|2; 5|8|; = 1 ⋅ 8 − 2 ⋅ 5; = − 2✓]

Multiplying a [MATH: n\times n] matrix by a scalar [MATH: k] is equivalent to multiplying each row by [MATH: k,] and this occurs [MATH: n] times. This leads to the result

[MATH: det(2A)|= 2^{4} ⋅ det(A); = 16 ⋅ 5; = 80.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

  • The operation [MATH: R_4 \leftrightarrow R_5] involves swapping two rows, so it changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.

  • The operation [MATH: R_6:= 4 R_6] involves multiplying a row by [MATH: 4,] so the determinant is multiplied by [MATH: 4] as well.

  • The operation [MATH: R_8:= R_8 - \dfrac{1}{2} R_7] involves adding a multiple of one row to another row, so it does not change the determinant.

Therefore, we have to change the sign of the determinant to the opposite one and multiply by [MATH: 4] as well. Consequently, we get

[MATH: det(B)|= 4 ⋅ (− det(A)); = − 4det(A); = − 4 ⋅ 5; = − 20.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Remember the following three standard elementary row operations:

Content:
I. Swapping two rows
II. Multiplying a row by a non-zero number
III. Adding a multiple of one row to another row

Content:
Of these three elementary row operations, only III (adding a multiple of one row to another row) preserves the determinant. The other two operations, switching two rows or multiplying a row by a non-zero number, change the determinant.

Content:
To demonstrate, let's consider the matrix [MATH: [1|2; 3|4]] Taking the determinant, we have
[MATH: 1|2; 3|4]

Content:
If we swap the two rows, we get a different determinant:
[MATH: |3|4; 1|2||= 3 ⋅ 2 − 1 ⋅ 4; = 2; ≠ − 2×]

Content:
Likewise, if we multiply top row by [MATH: {\color{red}2},] then we get a different determinant:
[MATH: |2 ⋅ 1|2 ⋅ 2; 3|4||=|2|4; 3|4|; = 2 ⋅ 4 − 3 ⋅ 4; = − 4; ≠ − 2×]

Content:
However, if we add twice the top row to the bottom row, then we get the same determinant:
[MATH: |1|2; 3 + 2 ⋅ 1|4 + 2 ⋅ 2||=|1|2; 5|8|; = 1 ⋅ 8 − 2 ⋅ 5; = − 2✓]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Switching Two Rows Changes the Sign of the Determinant

Content:
As we saw, swapping two rows does not preserve the determinant. However, the only difference is the sign of the determinant changes.

Content:
[MATH: |1|2; 3|4||= 1 ⋅ 4 − 2 ⋅ 3 = − 2;|3|4; 1|2||= 3 ⋅ 2 − 1 ⋅ 4 = 2]

Content:
So, in the above example, we have

Content:
[MATH: |1|2; 3|4||= −|3|4; 1|2|.]

Content:
In general, swapping any two rows of a matrix changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one. That is to say,
[MATH: det[⋮|⋮|…|⋮; ◻|◻|…|◻; ⋮|⋮|…|⋮; △|△|…|△; ⋮|⋮|…|⋮] = − det[⋮|⋮|…|⋮; △|△|…|△; ⋮|⋮|…|⋮; ◻|◻|…|◻; ⋮|⋮|…|⋮].]

---

Item 3 — Example: Calculating a Determinant After Switching Two Rows

Example Prompt:
Suppose [MATH: A] is a [MATH: 3 \times 3] matrix and [MATH: \det (A) = -16.] The matrix [MATH: B] is obtained from [MATH: A] by applying the elementary row operation [MATH: R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2] (switching the first and the second rows). What is the value of [MATH: \det(B)?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Since swapping any two rows changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite sign, we have

[MATH: det(B)|= − det(A); = − (− 16); = 16.]

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: Multiplying a Row By a Number Scales the Determinant By That Number

Content:
As we have seen, multiplying a row by a number does not preserve the determinant. However, it does affect the determinant in a predictable way: multiplying a row by a number scales the determinant by that number as well.

Content:
[MATH: |1|2; 3|4||= 1 ⋅ 4 − 2 ⋅ 3 = − 2;|2 ⋅ 1|2 ⋅ 2; 3|4|=|2|4; 3|4||= 2 ⋅ 4 − 3 ⋅ 4 = − 4]

Content:
So, in the above example, we have
[MATH: 2 ⋅ 1|2 ⋅ 2; 3|4]

Content:
In general, multiplying a row of a matrix by a number multiplies the determinant by that number. That is to say, we can factor out the common multiplier from the row of the determinant:
[MATH: det[⋮|⋮|…|⋮; k△|k△|…|k△; ⋮|⋮|…|⋮] = k ⋅ det[⋮|⋮|…|⋮; △|△|…|△; ⋮|⋮|…|⋮]]

---

Item 7 — Example: Calculating a Determinant After Multiplying a Row by a Number

Example Prompt:

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The row operation applied to [MATH: A] consists of multiplying a row by the number [MATH: \dfrac{1}{8}.]

When we do this, the determinant is multiplied by the same number. So, we have

[MATH: det(B)|= (1)/(8)det(A); = (1)/(8) ⋅ 32; = 4.]

Item 10 — Tutorial: Multiplying a Matrix By a Scalar

Content:
Let's check what happens if we multiply the entire matrix (not only one row) by a number. For example,

Content:
[MATH: |1|2; 3|4||= 1 ⋅ 4 − 2 ⋅ 3 = − 2;|3 ⋅ 1|3 ⋅ 2; 3 ⋅ 3|3 ⋅ 4|=|3|6; 9|12||= 3 ⋅ 12 − 6 ⋅ 9 = − 18]

Content:
So, in the above example, we have

Content:
[MATH: 3 ⋅ 1|3 ⋅ 2; 3 ⋅ 3|3 ⋅ 4]

Content:
The above is equivalent to multiplying both rows of the matrix by [MATH: 3]. Multiplying the first row scales the determinant by [MATH: 3], and then multiplying the second row scales it by [MATH: 3] once more.

Content:
In general, multiplying an entire [MATH: n \times n] matrix by a number multiplies the determinant by that number to the power of [MATH: n]. That is to say, we can factor out the common multiplier from the entire matrix, as follows:
[MATH: det(k ⋅ A) = k^{n} ⋅ det(A),]
where [MATH: A] is an [MATH: n \times n] matrix.

---

Item 11 — Example: Calculating a Determinant After Multiplying a Matrix by a Scalar

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Multiplying a [MATH: n\times n] matrix by a scalar [MATH: k] is equivalent to multiplying each row by [MATH: k,] and this occurs [MATH: n] times. This leads to the result

[MATH: det(k ⋅ A) = k^{n} ⋅ det(A).]

In our case, we have [MATH: k=2] and [MATH: n=4.] Therefore,

[MATH: det(2A)|= 2^{4} ⋅ det(A); = 16 ⋅ 5; = 80.]
